questions.prompt: After a step is applied to an RC low-pass filter, how long does the output take to reach about 63% of its final value?
questions.explanation: At \(t=\tau\): \(1-e^{-1}=0.632\), i.e., about 63% of the final value. After \(2\tau\) it is 86.5%, after \(5\tau\) it is 99.3% (essentially settled).
questions.figure_alt: Normalized RC step response rising toward 1.

questions.prompt: An amplifier is driven with a 2 mV amplitude sinusoid and the output amplitude is 0.5 V. What is the magnitude of its voltage gain \(|G_{v}|\)?
questions.explanation: \(|G_{v}|=|V_{\mathrm{out}}|/|V_{\mathrm{in}}|=0.5\ \mathrm{V}/0.002\ \mathrm{V}=250\). Since \(|G_{v}|>1\) the circuit has voltage gain (if it were below 1 it would attenuate). Common mistake: dividing in mV and V without converting units \((0.5/2=0.25)\).

questions.prompt: A resistive voltage divider has a 2 kΩ series resistor followed by a 6 kΩ resistor to ground. A 6 kΩ load is connected across the 6 kΩ resistor, and the output is taken across the load. What is \(G_{v}=V_{\mathrm{out}}/V_{\mathrm{in}}\)?
questions.explanation:
The load is in parallel with the 6 kΩ shunt resistor: \(6\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 6\ \mathrm{k}\Omega=3\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\). Then \(G_{v}=3k/(2k+3k)=0.6\).
• \(0.75=6k/(2k+6k)\) ignores the loading by the 6 kΩ load.
• \(0.4=2k/(2k+3k)\) divides in the wrong order (series resistor over the total).
• \(0.5=6k/(6k+6k)\) divides the input between the two 6 kΩ resistors and ignores the 2 kΩ series resistor.
A transfer function always depends on what is connected to the output.

questions.prompt: A series RLC circuit (passive: only R, L and C, with a voltage source) has \(Q=10\). Can the voltage across the capacitor be larger than the source voltage?
options: Yes: at resonance \(|V_{C}/V_{s}|=Q=10\). The circuit has voltage gain but no power gain
No: a passive circuit can only attenuate, so \(|V_{C}/V_{s}|\le 1\) at every frequency
Yes, and since the voltage is \(10\times\) larger, the circuit also has a power gain of 10
No: \(|V_{C}|=|V_{L}|\) always, so the capacitor and inductor voltages cancel and stay below the source
questions.explanation:
'Gain' of a transfer function just means \(|V_{\mathrm{out}}/V_{\mathrm{in}}|>1\); passive circuits can have it (reader Sec. 2.2.2 and 2.5.3). At resonance, I \(=V_{s}/R\), so \(|V_{C}|=|I|/(\omega_{0}C)=V_{s}\cdot Q\): the capacitor and inductor voltages are each Q times the source voltage (and 180° out of phase with each other, so they cancel in the KVL sum).
This is voltage gain, not power gain: the source supplies the power dissipated in R, and no more.
• Passive \(\ne\) attenuation-only for voltage ratios.
• Power gain would need an active element.
• \(V_{C}\) and \(V_{L}\) are equal in magnitude at resonance but each is Q times \(V_{s}\), which can be larger than the source.

questions.prompt: Two identical resistive dividers (each: 10 kΩ in series, then 10 kΩ to ground) are connected directly one after the other (no buffer). What is the overall \(V_{\mathrm{out}}/V_{\mathrm{in}}\) measured at the output of the second divider (open circuit)?
questions.explanation:
Each divider alone has \(G=10k/(10k+10k)=0.5\), but the gains do NOT simply multiply (0.25), because the second divider loads the first.
The first divider's shunt resistor sees 10 kΩ in parallel with the second divider's input resistance \((10k+10k=20\ \mathrm{k}\Omega)\): \(10k\parallel 20k=6.667\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\).
\(G_{1}=6.667k/(10k+6.667k)=0.4\). The second stage (unloaded) has \(G_{2}=0.5\). Total \(=0.4\times 0.5=0.2\).
(Nodal analysis confirms 0.2.) Cascading transfer functions requires including the loading effect.

questions.prompt: Preview of the common-source amplifier. A transistor produces a drain current \(i_{d}=g_{m}\cdot v_{\mathrm{gs}}\), a transadmittance of \(g_{m}=2\ \mathrm{mS}\) (this current flows from the supply through \(R_{D}=5\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) to the drain, so \(v_{\mathrm{out}}=-i_{d}\cdot R_{D}\)). The small-signal input is \(v_{\mathrm{gs}}=10\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{mV}\). What is \(v_{\mathrm{out}}\)?
questions.explanation:
Chain the two transfer functions: first a transadmittance (voltage → current), then a transimpedance with gain \(-R_{D}\) (current → voltage).
\(i_{d}=2\ \mathrm{mS}\times 10\ \mathrm{mV}=20\ \mu\mathrm{A}\); \(v_{\mathrm{out}}=-20\ \mu\mathrm{A}\times 5\ \mathrm{k}\Omega=-100\ \mathrm{mV}\). The overall voltage gain is \(-g_{m}\ R_{D}=-10\ \mathrm{V}/\mathrm{V}\) (an inverting amplifier, phase 180°).
• +100 mV misses the inversion.
• −20 mV forgets to multiply by \(R_{D}\ (20\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) is the current, not a voltage).
• −10 mV is the gain \(-g_{m}R_{D}\) with no input amplitude applied.
